entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a continuous-time input-output system as linear time-invariant by applying the superposition and time-shift tests together, establishing when the impulse-response and convolution framework applies.

sections.lesson_title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
sections.section_title: Testing a Constant-Gain System for LTI Classification

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=-2x(t)$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A constant gain is still a linear rule, and the same fixed factor appears after any time shift, so both superposition and time invariance hold. The negative sign does not change that, so the system is LTI.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A fixed fractional gain still preserves addition, scaling, and time shifts. Since the coefficient does not depend on t, the system is linear and time-invariant.

sections.lesson_title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
sections.section_title: Testing a Derivative System for LTI Classification

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=5\,dx(t)/dt$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A constant multiplier does not change the derivative rule into anything nonlinear or time-varying. Differentiation preserves superposition and commutes with shifts, so the system is LTI.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\,dx(t)/dt$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative fractional gain is still just a fixed constant, so it preserves scaling and addition. Since the derivative itself also preserves time shifts, the system is LTI.

sections.lesson_title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
sections.section_title: Rejecting LTI Classification When Linearity Fails

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=|x(t)|$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Absolute value is a pointwise nonlinear operation, so superposition fails and the system cannot be LTI. But the rule has no explicit t, so shifting the input just shifts the output. The correct classification is nonlinear but time-invariant.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=x^3(t)$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Cubing breaks superposition, so the system is not linear and therefore not LTI. The rule depends only on $x(t)$ and has no explicit t, so shifting the input still just shifts the output. The correct classification is nonlinear but time-invariant.

sections.lesson_title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
sections.section_title: Rejecting LTI Classification When Time Invariance Fails

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=(t+2)x(t)$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The multiplier depends only on t, so the rule is linear in $x(t)$. But after a time shift, the multiplier should become t-$t_0$, and that does not match the original shifted output. So the system is linear but time-varying, not LTI.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the system $y(t)=\cos(t)x(t)$ as LTI, linear but time-varying, nonlinear but time-invariant, or nonlinear and time-varying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Cosine is just a time-dependent multiplier, so the system is still linear in the input. But shifting the input changes the comparison from $\cos$(t) to $\cos$(t-$t_0$), so the time-shift test fails. The correct classification is linear but time-varying.

sections.lesson_title: Linear Time-Invariant Systems
sections.section_title: Deciding Whether the Impulse-Response Framework Applies

prompt_blocks.text: Decide whether the impulse-response framework applies to the system $y(t)=x(t)+x(t-2)$.

choice_blocks.text: framework applies because the system is LTI
does not apply because linearity fails
does not apply because time invariance fails
does not apply because both tests fail

questions.correct_answer: framework applies because the system is LTI

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This rule is a linear combination of the current input and a delayed copy of the input, so it passes superposition. The same fixed delay also passes the time-shift test. Since the system is LTI, the impulse-response framework applies.

prompt_blocks.text: Decide whether the impulse-response framework applies to the system $y(t)=4x(t)-x(t-1)$.

choice_blocks.text: framework applies because the system is LTI
does not apply because linearity fails
does not apply because time invariance fails
does not apply because both tests fail

questions.correct_answer: framework applies because the system is LTI

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output is still a linear combination of the present input and a shifted input, so the system is linear. The fixed shift behaves the same after any input shift, so time invariance also holds. Because the system is LTI, the impulse-response framework applies.

entries.lesson_title: Why Linearity and Time Invariance Matter Together
entries.lesson_core_move: Justify why linearity and time invariance must be paired by tracing how shifted and scaled input components produce shifted and scaled copies of one reusable impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: Why Linearity and Time Invariance Matter Together
sections.section_title: Tracing a Scaled Input Component Through a Linear System

prompt_blocks.text: A linear system satisfies $T{x(t)} = y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input $-2x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Linearity means the same scalar on the input must appear on the output. Since $T{x(t)} = y(t)$, scaling the input by -2 gives $T{-2x(t)} = -2T{x(t)} = -2y(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: A linear system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input 1/4 $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: By homogeneity, a scalar on the input transfers unchanged to the output. Since $T{x(t)} = y(t)$, the input $\frac{1}{4}x(t)$ produces $T{\frac{1}{4}x(t)} = \frac{1}{4}T{x(t)} = \frac{1}{4}y(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Why Linearity and Time Invariance Matter Together
sections.section_title: Tracing a Shifted Input Component Through a Time-Invariant System

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose a time-invariant system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input $x(t + 3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time invariance copies the same shift from input to output. Since $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$, the shifted input $x(t + 3)$ must produce the shifted output $y(t + 3)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose a time-invariant system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input $x(t - 5)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time-invariant system preserves the direction and size of the time shift. Because the input is delayed by 5, the output must be the same delayed copy: $y(t - 5)$.

sections.lesson_title: Why Linearity and Time Invariance Matter Together
sections.section_title: Tracing a Scaled and Shifted Component Through an LTI System

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose an LTI system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input $4x(t + 1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is both scaled and shifted. Time invariance sends $x(t + 1)$ to $y(t + 1)$, and linearity carries the factor 4 through unchanged. The output is $4y(t + 1)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose an LTI system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. What output must correspond to the input $-3x(t - 2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First trace the shift: $x(t - 2)$ must become $y(t - 2)$. Then carry the scalar -3 through by linearity. The combined output is $-3y(t - 2)$.

sections.lesson_title: Why Linearity and Time Invariance Matter Together
sections.section_title: Justifying a Reusable Response Pattern for LTI Systems

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system satisfies $T{x(t)}$ = $y(t)$. Which statement best explains why the outputs for $5x(t)$, $x(t - 6)$, and $5x(t - 6)$ can all be predicted from $y(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: Because linearity alone predicts $5x(t)$ gives $5y(t)$, so the same response pattern covers all three inputs.
Because time invariance alone predicts $x(t - 6)$ gives $y(t - 6)$, so the same response pattern covers all three inputs.
Because the input changes but the output stays $y(t)$, unshifted and unscaled.
Because a new response must be measured for every shifted or scaled input component.
Because linearity gives $5y(t)$ for $5x(t)$, time invariance gives $y(t - 6)$ for $x(t - 6)$, and together they give $5y(t - 6)$ for $5x(t - 6)$.

questions.correct_answer: Because linearity gives $5y(t)$ for $5x(t)$, time invariance gives $y(t - 6)$ for $x(t - 6)$, and together they give $5y(t - 6)$ for $5x(t - 6)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The reusable response pattern works only because both properties are available. Linearity handles the scale factor, time invariance handles the shift, and together they let you predict the transformed outputs from $y(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system satisfies $T{x(t)} = y(t)$. Which statement best explains why the outputs for $-2x(t)$, $x(t + 4)$, and $-2x(t + 4)$ can all be predicted from $y(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: Because linearity alone gives $-2y(t)$, so no shift rule is needed.
Because time invariance alone gives $y(t + 4)$, so no scale rule is needed.
Because the output for $-2x(t + 4)$ stays $y(t)$ unchanged.
Because a new response must be measured for $-2x(t + 4)$ even if $y(t)$ is known.
Because linearity gives $-2y(t)$, time invariance gives $y(t + 4)$, and together they give $-2y(t + 4)$.

questions.correct_answer: Because linearity gives $-2y(t)$, time invariance gives $y(t + 4)$, and together they give $-2y(t + 4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A reusable response pattern needs both properties. Linearity carries the factor -2, time invariance carries the advance by 4, and the combined output is the same known response pattern with both changes applied.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret the unit impulse input delta(t) as the canonical probe whose output from an LTI system becomes the reference response used for later shifted and scaled impulse inputs.

sections.lesson_title: The Unit Impulse Input
sections.section_title: Identifying delta(t) as the Probe Input

prompt_blocks.text: Which candidate is the unshifted unit impulse probe input?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The probe input is the unshifted unit impulse. Only $\delta(t)$ is both an impulse and located at $t = 0$ with unit weight. The step, shifted impulse, scaled impulse, and rectangular pulse all fail one of those checks.

prompt_blocks.text: Which candidate is the canonical probe input?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The canonical probe input is $\delta(t)$. It is the only option that is an impulse, is unshifted, and has unit weight. The other choices each change one feature of the probe input, such as amplitude, shift, or signal type.

sections.lesson_title: The Unit Impulse Input
sections.section_title: Distinguishing the Impulse Input from Its System Output

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, an input arrow labeled delta(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system. On the right, an output arrow labeled r(t) leaves the block and points to a distinct smooth decaying response waveform. Make the arrow directions unambiguous. Do not show h(t), convolution, shifted impulses, or scaled impulses.

A clean top-to-bottom block diagram. At the top, a downward input arrow labeled delta(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system. At the bottom, a downward output arrow labeled y(t) exits the block and points to a distinct smooth decaying response waveform. Make the input and output directions unambiguous. Do not show h(t), convolution, shifted impulses, or scaled impulses.

prompt_blocks.text: A block diagram shows $\delta(t)$ entering an LTI system and $r(t)$ leaving it. Which statement correctly identifies the input and output?

choice_blocks.text: $r(t)$ is the input and $\delta(t)$ is the output.
$\delta(t)$ is the input and $r(t)$ is the output.
The LTI system block is the output signal.

questions.correct_answer: $\delta(t)$ is the input and $r(t)$ is the output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The arrow entering the system carries the applied input, so $\delta(t)$ is the probe signal. The arrow leaving the system carries the output produced by that input, so $r(t)$ is the system response.

prompt_blocks.text: A block diagram shows $\delta(t)$ entering an LTI system and $y(t)$ leaving it. Which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $\delta(t)$ is the output and $y(t)$ is the input.
The LTI system block is the output signal.
$\delta(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output.
$y(t)$ is the impulse input and $\delta(t)$ is the output.

questions.correct_answer: $\delta(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal on the entering arrow is the applied input, and the signal on the leaving arrow is the response produced by the system. The label $y(t)$ names the output, while $\delta(t)$ names the impulse input probe.

sections.lesson_title: The Unit Impulse Input
sections.section_title: Using the Unit Impulse Output as the Reference Response

image_slots.image_description: A clean left-to-right block diagram. On the left, an input arrow labeled delta(t) enters a rectangle labeled LTI system. On the right, an output arrow labeled r(t) leaves the block and points to a distinct smooth response waveform. Add a light annotation next to r(t) that says reference response for later impulse inputs. Do not show shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or convolution notation.

A clean top-to-bottom block diagram. At the top, an input arrow labeled delta(t) points downward into a rectangle labeled LTI system. At the bottom, an output arrow labeled g(t) points downward out of the block and leads to a distinct smooth response waveform. Add a light annotation next to g(t) that says reference response for later impulse inputs. Do not show shifted impulses, scaled impulses, or convolution notation.

prompt_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the input $\delta(t)$ produces the output $r(t)$. What is the correct interpretation of $r(t)$ in this lesson?

choice_blocks.text: $r(t)$ is the input signal rather than the output.
$r(t)$ is arbitrary and cannot be reused for the system.
$r(t)$ already represents the response to a shifted impulse.
$r(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: $r(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is the unit impulse $\delta(t)$, and the signal leaving the system is the output. In this lesson, that output is not just any response; it is the reference response that later impulse inputs will reuse.

prompt_blocks.text: A different LTI system produces $g(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t)$. What does $g(t)$ represent here?

choice_blocks.text: $g(t)$ is the input signal rather than the output.
$g(t)$ is arbitrary and cannot be reused for the system.
$g(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.
$g(t)$ already represents the response to a shifted impulse.
A step input, rather than a unit impulse input, defines this reference response.

questions.correct_answer: $g(t)$ is the reference response produced by $\delta(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The symbol can change, but the role does not. If $\delta(t)$ produces $g(t)$, then $g(t)$ is the output tied to the unit impulse probe, so it serves as the reference response for later impulse-input reasoning.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine an LTI system's impulse response h(t) by evaluating its output to delta(t) and interpreting that output as the kernel that governs shifted, scaled, and decomposed impulse inputs.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Finding h(t) from a Given Delta-Input Output

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has the output shown below when the input is $x(t) = \delta(t)$. Find $h(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the input is $\delta(t)$, the given output is the impulse response.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has the output shown below when the input is $x(t) = \delta(t)$. Find $h(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(t) = \delta(t)$, the system output is $h(t)$, so we copy the given expression.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Finding h(t) by Applying a System Rule to delta(t)

prompt_blocks.text: For the LTI system below, find $h(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $x(t)=\delta(t)$. Then $x(t-2)$ becomes $\delta(t-2)$, so the output to $\delta(t)$ is the impulse response.

prompt_blocks.text: For the LTI system below, find $h(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace $x(t)$ with $\delta(t)$. The shifted term $x(t-3)$ becomes $\delta(t-3)$, so the resulting output is $h(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Distinguishing the Impulse Input from the Impulse Response

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=4e^{-3t}u(t)$. Which expression is the impulse response?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The impulse response is the output named by $h(t)$, so the expression after $h(t)$= is the correct choice. $\delta(t)$ is the probe input, and $x(t)$ is a generic input symbol, not the impulse response.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system is described by $h(t)=e$^{-t}$u(t)$. Which expression is the impulse input?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The impulse input is the unit impulse that probes the system, so $\delta(t)$ is the correct label. $e^{-t}$$u(t)$ is the output response $h(t)$, and $y(t)$ is just the ordinary output symbol.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Interpreting h(t) as the Reference Response for Later Impulse Inputs

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has output $y(t)=2e^{-4t}u(t)$ when $x(t)=\delta(t)$. Identify $h(t)$ and state its role for later shifted or scaled impulse inputs.

questions.correct_answer: $h(t)=2e^{-4t}u(t)$; it is the reference response for later shifted or scaled impulse inputs.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the unit impulse is the input, the resulting output is the system's impulse response. So the given output expression becomes $h(t)$, and that same response pattern is the reference used when later impulse inputs are shifted or scaled.
This is the reference response, not a later transformed output yet.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has output $y(t)=5e^{-2t}u(t)$ when $x(t)=\delta(t)$. Identify $h(t)$ and state its role for later shifted or scaled impulse inputs.

questions.correct_answer: $h(t)=5e^{-2t}u(t)$; it is the reference response for later shifted or scaled impulse inputs.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: When the input is $\delta(t)$, the output is named $h(t)$. That output is the system's reference response, which later impulse inputs will reuse after shifting or scaling.
The task is to name the reference response and its role, not to compute any modified response yet.

entries.lesson_title: Impulse Response as a System Description
entries.lesson_core_move: Use the impulse response h(t) as a complete LTI-system description by mapping shifted and scaled impulse components to corresponding shifted and scaled copies of h(t).

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response as a System Description
sections.section_title: Reading h(t) as the Response Template for the Unit Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For the unit impulse input $\delta(t)$, the output of an LTI system is its impulse response itself. Since the given impulse response is $h(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$, that is the output.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=5e^{-2t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit impulse $\delta(t)$. By definition, the output to $\delta(t)$ is the impulse response itself, with no shift or scale applied.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response as a System Description
sections.section_title: Mapping a Time-Shifted Impulse Component to a Time-Shifted Copy of h(t)

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t-2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time shift in the input impulse produces the same time shift in the impulse response. So $\delta(t-2)$ maps to $h(t-2)$, and then you substitute $t-2$ into the given formula for $h(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t-5)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is a delayed unit impulse, so the output is the same response template delayed by 5. That means the output is $h(t-5)$, with $t-5$ substituted into the original formula.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response as a System Description
sections.section_title: Mapping an Amplitude-Scaled Impulse Component to an Amplitude-Scaled Copy of h(t)

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $4\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A scale factor on the impulse input scales the entire output by the same factor. Since the input is $4\delta(t)$, the output is $4h(t)$, and then you substitute the given formula for $h(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=3e^{-2t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $-2\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Linearity means the output keeps the same scalar factor as the input impulse. The negative sign stays on the output, so the response is $-2h(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Impulse Response as a System Description
sections.section_title: Mapping a Scaled and Shifted Impulse Component to a Scaled and Shifted Copy of h(t)

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=2e^{-4t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $4\delta(t-1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input has both a scale factor and a delay. By linearity and time invariance, $4\delta(t-1)$ maps to $4h(t-1)$, and then you substitute $t-1$ into the given formula for $h(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)=5e^{-t}u(t)$. What is the output when the input is $-3\delta(t-2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the scalar and the delay together: the coefficient $-3$ multiplies the whole response, and the delay $2$ shifts the response to $h(t-2)$. Then expand the given $h(t)$.

entries.lesson_title: Shifted Impulses Through an LTI System
entries.lesson_core_move: Map a shifted impulse input delta(t - tau) to the correspondingly shifted impulse response h(t - tau) by applying time invariance within the LTI impulse-response framework.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for a Delayed Unit Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t - 5)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delayed unit impulse still produces the impulse response, shifted by the same amount. Time invariance carries the input delay of 5 directly to the output.
So the output is $y(t) = h(t - 5)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t - 2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is still a unit impulse, just delayed by 2. For an LTI system, the output keeps the same delay because time invariance preserves shifts.
Therefore $y(t) = h(t - 2)$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for an Advanced Unit Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t + 4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A plus sign in $\delta(t + 4)$ means the impulse is advanced by 4. Time invariance says the same shift carries to the impulse response, so treat the input as $\delta(t - (-4)$).
Simplifying the output argument gives $y(t) = h(t + 4)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $\delta(t + 1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is still a unit impulse, but it is shifted left by 1. For an LTI system, that same advance appears on the output response.
So the output is $y(t) = h(t + 1)$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Mapping a Symbolic Shift Through the Impulse Response

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t - T)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shift T stays symbolic. Time invariance means the same shift on the input impulse must appear on the impulse response.
So $\delta(t - T)$ maps directly to $h(t - T)$, and the output is $y(t) = h(t - T)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output when the input is $\delta(t - a)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Do not replace the symbol a with a number. The input is just a shifted unit impulse, so the output keeps the same symbolic shift.
Therefore $y(t) = h(t - a)$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Matching the Input Shift to the Output Shift

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. Which output matches the input $\delta(t + 6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plus sign means the impulse is advanced by 6. For an LTI system, the output keeps the same shift on the impulse response.
So the matching output is $h(t + 6)$, not the unchanged response, the sign-reversed response, the wrong shift amount, or the impulse itself.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. Which output matches the input $\delta(t + 2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A plus sign in the input means an advanced impulse. Time invariance copies that same shift onto the response.
So the correct output is $h(t + 2)$.

entries.lesson_title: Scaled Impulses Through an LTI System
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output of an LTI system for a scaled shifted impulse by applying homogeneity and time invariance to convert a delta(t - t0) into a h(t - t0).

sections.lesson_title: Scaled Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for a Scaled Unshifted Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 5$ $\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is a positive scalar multiple of the unshifted impulse. By homogeneity, the factor 5 copies onto the impulse response.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $5h(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 2$ $\delta(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same unshifted-impulse rule with a different scalar. The factor 2 multiplies the impulse response because the system is linear.
Therefore the output is $y(t)$ = $2h(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Scaled Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for a Scaled Delayed Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 2$ $\delta(t - 4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input is a scaled delayed impulse. Time invariance carries the delay 4 to the impulse response, and homogeneity carries the factor 2 along with it.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $2h(t - 4)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 7$ $\delta(t - 1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same delayed-impulse rule with a different positive scalar. The minus sign inside the impulse argument stays a minus sign in the output argument.
Therefore the output is $y(t)$ = $7h(t - 1)$.

sections.lesson_title: Scaled Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for a Scaled Advanced Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 3$ $\delta(t + 2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plus sign means the impulse is advanced by 2, so time invariance shifts the impulse response to $h(t + 2)$ and homogeneity keeps the factor 3.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $3h(t + 2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = 4$ $\delta(t + 1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is a scaled advanced impulse. The advance by 1 carries over to the impulse response, and the factor 4 stays attached to the output.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $4h(t + 1)$.

sections.lesson_title: Scaled Impulses Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding the Output for a Negative Scaled Shifted Impulse

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = -4$ $\delta(t + 1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The minus sign stays as a multiplier on the output. The plus sign in $\delta(t + 1)$ means a shift left by 1, so the impulse response becomes $h(t + 1)$.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $-4h(t + 1)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has impulse response $h(t)$. What is the output $y(t)$ when the input is $x(t) = -3$ $\delta(t + 2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the negative sign on the amplitude and carry the advance by 2 into the time argument of $h(t)$.
So the output is $y(t)$ = $-3h(t + 2)$.
